title: Rohatsu again
hook: the week of sitting for the awakening

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lhabab Duchen: a debt to a mother, repaid with the teaching. Your line was he came down. How did you honor the one who mothered you? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

The last night of the week. In a cold Zen hall, nobody has lain down. The candles are low. Legs ache. Someone's stomach growls, loud, and nobody laughs. Then the windows begin to gray, and low in the east, before the sun, one bright point of light hangs over the trees. In Zen tellings, that is the moment: the seeker under the tree looks up at the morning star and wakes. Rohatsu is the week of sitting that ends there. You've stayed through the last night before, and through the middle of the week with Mara's army. This year, listen for what tradition says came out of his mouth when it was over.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT OF THE WEEK.` → `ONE BRIGHT POINT IN THE EAST.` → `WHAT DID HE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, the verses. The Dhammapada holds two short verses that the commentary tradition places on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening. He speaks to a builder: the one who keeps putting up the house of a self, life after life. He says he went looking for that builder through many births, and birth again and again was painful. Second, the turn. In Max Müller's words: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent or a house. The verse goes on to say the rafters are broken and the ridge-pole shattered. Third, who the builder is. The commentary reads the builder as the mind's own craving, the thirst that keeps reaching and keeps making a shelter out of me and mine. It was never an enemy outside. It was a habit, and once it was seen clearly, it couldn't keep building. Fourth, why a week of sitting. The house is not taken down by force. It's seen. And seeing needs stillness, so for a week, from before dawn into the night, people in Zen halls sit and watch the builder at work: the plans, the worries, the little stories of who they are. Then the morning star. This week on the path has walked the festival year: the wheel set rolling, the rains, the ancestors, the invitation, the gifts, the descent. It ends where the teaching began: one person, sitting still until the morning star.
screen: `TWO VERSES AT THE AWAKENING.` · `THE BUILDER HAS BEEN SEEN.` · `CRAVING BUILDS THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Sit as still as is comfortable, and let the breath settle. Then watch for the builder. A thought arrives, a plan for later, a worry about someone, a story about yourself. Don't fight it. Just notice: there's the builder, picking up a plank. Let it go, and come back to the breath. Again and again. When the bell rings, if you have time, keep sitting. Ten more minutes, if you can, the way the Zen halls stay through the night. If not, even one more breath counts. The bell holds the time.
Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the awakening, when tradition says the Buddha saw the morning star. Today's word.
Your line: the morning star. Tomorrow before sunrise, if the sky is clear, look east for one bright point and take one slow breath. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries in Japan and elsewhere, monks and lay practitioners sit an intensive week-long retreat called Rohatsu sesshin, ending on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, sometimes sitting through the final night.

original.note: Pali gahakaraka: house-builder, the one the Buddha addresses in Dhammapada 153–154.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rohatsu is a long meditation retreat.
what it means: a week of sitting to watch the builder at work, ending on the morning of the awakening.
what a scholar hears: the house-builder verses, Dhammapada 153–154, placed by the commentary at the awakening, and the Zen morning star.

sources.quoted: But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again.

sources.ref: Japanese Zen practice of Rohatsu sesshin; the morning star in East Asian tellings

notes: Dhammapada 154 opening quoted from Müller (1881); confirm wording exactly ('But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again.').
Dh 153–154 paraphrased: seeking the house-builder through many births; rafters broken, ridge-pole shattered. Identifying the builder as craving (tanha) follows the commentarial reading; confirm.
'The commentary tradition places [these verses] on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening': confirm phrasing; some traditions place a different utterance first.
Morning star at the awakening attributed to Zen / East Asian tellings.
Original: Devanagari for Pali gahakaraka (गहकारक); confirm spelling.
'Ten more minutes' comes from the outline's practice ('sit an extra ten minutes'); it is an invitation, not a claim.
Week end (days 1415–1421): the teach's close looks back over the week. Earlier Rohatsu days (y2 691, y3 1058) used the last night and the Padhana Sutta; this day uses the house-builder verses.

Editor: the verse itself does not name craving as the builder; attributed that reading to the commentary (teach and myth reveal). Replaced "the awakening they all point back to" (overclaims Ullambana and the descent) with a plain close.
